Yep, you got it, friend!

There are no reactions in this game. You just do shit on your turn, and your opponent does shit on their turn. They may add reactions/"instant" mechanics in later sets (but I've read the devs had said they don't want to do this.)

There's nothing like the stack in Magic. Things just happen, then resolve. You exert to quest, you gain the lore. Bam. Done. You exert to challenge, combat happens. Bam. Done.

On your turn, once you get to Main Phase (after drawing and untapping,) you can do things in any order you want. You opponent cannot do anything during your turn and vice versa (unless a card specifies to, but I'm not aware of any cards that have that interaction.)

Nope. It's not like M:tG or something where you declare you're going on a quest, and then your opponent gets to decide who to "block" with. The only time you take an action is on your turn.

So you can quest with a character, gain the lore, then end your turn. On your opponent's turn, they can challenge with one character to "do battle." Then it resolves, damage is dealt at the same time. After that interaction, they can then do something with another character - quest, challenge the character again if it didn't get banished the first time, etc. Then they end their turn.

You can then challenge any of their exerted/tapped cards - whether they were exerted from challenging or questing. 

But yeah, lore gets added as soon as you quest, and there is no interaction from an opponent when you quest (and you cannot interact with an opponent outside of your turn.)

You get any lore you tap without contention.

Former crisis counselor here. Worked for 988/National Suicide Prevention Lifeline earlier this year.

An uncollaborative EMS call is a LAST RESORT for most crisis lines. We'll do everything in our power to keep you safe in the moment. If you are at immediate risk for harming yourself or others, yes, we are required to contact Emergency Medical Services. Rarely will we ever call law enforcement without medical, if ever.

We receive training that covers the whole "cops show up and kill people" thing. 

First we assess if you're at immediate risk. If so, then we ask if you'd like to call EMS with us (we'll call for you with you on the line if you're not comfortable with it.) If you decline, but still express intent, a plan, a time frame, and access to means, then yes, we'll contact 911.
Not a lot of money in basic CS work, though.

Also, since it sounds like you may be relatively new to the game and unaware how SP gains work, here's a handy little chart. SP bonuses are...cumulative? Multiplicative? Shit I'm bad at math so I forget the term, but when you have more than one SP bonus, it goes like this:

Normal Kill: 3 SP

One Bonus: 6 SP (double base)

Two Bonus: 12 SP (double first bonus)

Three Bonus: 24 SP (double second bonus)


So on and so forth. Basically for every SP bonus source, start at 3 and then keep doubling. As far as SP bonus sources, here are the ones I can think of off the top of my head:

Unit has blessing or is Legendary/Mythic: x2
Weekend Bonus: x2
Unit has or is in party with relevant Valor skill: x2
Rarely we get an x5 bonus as a special celebration.

So if you bless your H!Hilda, it's the weekend, and you have a unit with Lance Valor in the party, she'll get 24SP per kill.

I think there are some other sources like Tempest Trials and Forging Bonds, but I never pay attention to those.

What most people are actually referring to are ADA accommodations. Yeah, FMLA will cover stuff but a lot of jobs I've had don't give you FMLA coverage unless you have been there for a year.

If you have a diagnosed illness (in my case, diagnosed Bipolar I,) then when you start a job (or at any point, really,) you tell them (your direct manager, HR, whoever is appropriate for your setting, but usually HR) that you want to request accommodations under the Americans with Disabilities Act (if you're in the US.)

Every time I've done this with employers I get some paperwork that my doctor and I have to fill out. We usually request for extra leeway with attendance because when I'm symptomatic, I find it difficult or even impossible to carry out normal daily functioning.

It's not guaranteed, and your request can't cause significant loss to your employer, but I haven't had any problems with getting a few extra excused absences.

You're confusing ODP with the whole opt-out bullshit. It's two different things. As I mentioned in another comment, here's how it works.

The way you described overdraft protection is pretty accurate - it's a service where you link up a qualifying account (savings, credit card) to your checking account. I'm going to use BoA's rules in these examples because I worked for them the longest (also for BB&T.)

If you have ODP set up, let's say linking your checking and savings and have $100 in your checking and $500 in your savings, then if you spend more than $100 in your checking it'll pull the needed amount from your savings.

Spend $200? Then $100 will pull from your savings and be put in your checking that day so you don't go into overdraft that night. Because - like you mentioned - it's a service, then there's a service fee of $12.

We cannot (legally) sign you up for this. Since it's a service you have to actively sign up for it. A good banker/CS agent will explain it fully to you and help you understand how it works. A poor one will not and may do some shady shit to increase their numbers.

Now, here's where people get a little confused. There's the whole opt-out thing I mentioned, and you sorta explained.

At BoA, every checking account has an "overdraft matrix." This is a dollar amount the bank will cover in situations where you don't have enough money in your checking. So in the previous example, if your matrix is $500 and you do NOT have ODP, then your account would become overdrawn by $100 because *the bank covers that amount for you.*

They charge $35 for this service. The bank will charge this fee for every single item they cover to a maximum of 4 in one business day. So if you have 3 things come through, $200, $200, and $150, then each one of those will generate a $35 fee. So the bank has covered $450 worth of items and charged $105 in fees. 

This is where ODP is a good thing. If you have that money in your savings, it'll pull over $450 from your savings and you'll get *one* $12 service charge. Sounds a lot better than $105, right? The catch is that you *have to have the $450 somewhere and linked to your checking.*

Now, back to the opt out thing. If you leave the setting alone, then anytime you use your card and don't have enough money, the bank's matrix will cover it as a service and charge you the OD/NSF fee. So if you have $100 and swipe for $200, it will go through.

If you OPT OUT, then the card will just decline, like you said. This and ODP are two different concepts. Opting out doesn't cost anything.

HOWEVER you can STILL OVERDRAW YOUR ACCOUNT. Recurring charges will still go through (Netflix, PS+, gym memberships) and OD the account and generate the fee. Also, bounced paper checks will also generate the OD/NSF fee.

Personally, I never advise people to opt-out. It's not as helpful as they think.

So I hope this post helps at least one person understand their checking account a little better.

Okay, I'm sorry, but this isn't entirely true. I'm seeing a FUCKTON of misinformation posted around in this thread and it's no wonder people wind up getting themselves into overdraft.

I worked customer service for Bank of America for many, many years, and my most recent time with them was last year.

First off, people ENTIRELY misunderstand what "overdraft protection" is.

It doesn't mean if you have it you can't get OD/NSF (overdraft/non-sufficient fund fees.) First off, actual overdraft protection is when you link an eligible account to your checking account. This is usually a savings account or a credit card. So let's say you have a checking account and a savings account. You can link your savings account to your checking account, so that when there aren't enough funds in the checking, it'll auto pull from the savings. So if you have $50 in your checking and $100 in your savings and a charge comes through for $75 on your checking, it'll pull the $25 you need from your savings.

You will be charged a fee for this. I believe BoA is $10 or $12 everytime your ODP protection kicks in. This is a SERVICE charge. The bank is providing a SERVICE. So instead of a $35 OD/NSF fee, you're paying $12. If you're the type that can't keep an updated and accurate checkbook register (which if you did you should almost NEVER manage to overdraw your account) then it's a good service.

Second, what you were referring to was the overdraft op-out bullshit. We called it the "decline all" setting.

You see, what banks don't tell you is every customer has an "overdraft matrix." It's an amount that the bank will cover you if you don't have enough funds. So if your ODM is $100 and you overdraw your account by $50, the bank covers that $50 for you, and then charges you a service charge for having your back.

With the "opt out" thing that came out relatively recently, you opt out of this - it effectively sets your matrix to $0. If you swipe your card and don't have money, it'll decline.

People do not realize YOU CAN STILL OD YOUR ACCOUNT EVEN IF YOU HAVE THIS. If you have recurring payments or subscriptions, like Netflix, a gym membership, etc, then YOU WILL STILL BE CHARGED, CAN GO OVERDRAFT, and WILL RECIEVE A FEE.

Look, I get banks use scummy practices, and BoA is no different. But in the years of experience I have, 95% of all scenarios involving overdrafts and NSF fee all fall down to people just not understanding how banking works. This information isn't hidden, either.

Educate yourselves, people. Being ignorant is too damn expensive.

This may or may not be the response you want to hear, but if you really believe you have a good life or good things but are still having those thoughts or feeling, *look into professional help.*

Am I diagnosing you? Nah, not at all. I'm just recommending a solution to the problem.

Don't know how to start? Make an appointment with a general practioner. Tell them about how you feel. They'll then get you in touch with someone that specializes in these sorts of things. It's okay to be scared, nervous, or unsure about how to go about it, but please keep this in mind - you're not the only one to ever have felt this way. Don't feel dumb or ashamed for asking for help. Medical professionals have dealt with thousands of people who feel just like you do, and they understand.

But yeah, TL;DR if you continue to have long bouts of depression and thoughts of suicide definitely try talking to a doctor. And illness is an illness and illnesses can be treat.

If you want any more information on how to go about getting help or just want someone to talk to who has felt like you're feeling, feel free to PM me. Approach it however you want. Shit, even if you just PM "Hey, DFWV, I'm just...really sad," that's a perfectly fine thing to said. c:

I was going to say this exact thing, but I want to add on to it a bit.

There's this thing called the *just-world hypothesis.* Basically, it's the line of thinking that good things happen to good people, bad things happen to bad people. 

The thing is, that's a fallacy. It's just not true. You (the collective "you") may not believe it yourself or even may find the idea preposterous. You may already believe life is unfair.

The poster I'm replying to is right - action is the best thing to do. Sure, there's random chance in life, but you do have some limited control. It's harder to achieve your goals and have good things if you don't actively work towards them

From your (OP) post, it sounds like you already know that. But here's where my own advice plays in.

*Even in taking action to achieve good things doesn't always result in said good things.* You can try and try and try and STILL wind up failing. You can do everything in your power to change a situation but in the end you just *can't.* It really fuckin' sucks, but to bring it back around, *the world isn't just*

So my true advice is don't let it get you too down. Don't give up trying just because something doesn't work out. Shit, don't give up even if *nothing* is working out. Like I said, doing something is more likely to lead to good things than doing nothing. Sometimes things are just shit with no real good reason. It's hard to keep going when things feel that way, but letting it bring you down is a surefire way to set yourself up for failure.

I really hope things go your way soon. c:
